rv.q: Bringing together romance, humor and swashbuckling swordfights, this is a production not to be missed.

As fun as the production elements of 'yo ho.' are, it's hard to call this an unqualified success when the leaner, meaner, one-act version of this play haunts its current iteration like the Flying Dutchman.

While there are a lot of laughs in this production, between the continual scene shifts, costume changes and the chaotic physical demands of the script, many scenes seem filled with pandemonium and confusion.

In general, yo ho. can feel disproportionately unserious compared with its technical ambition: the energy is closer to an enthusiastic college-theater production than the fully realized historical fantasy its marketing material promises.
What the production lacks, however, is a coherent narrative—or, to be blunt, a clear point; pun(s) intended.
The play is so determined to say everything that it struggles to say anything clearly.

They wear heavy boots, striped pants, with a beard across their face. Nothing seems amiss here, pirates have swords and no one has time to shave when there is much plundering, pillaging, and looting to be had. But looking closer, that shadow of a beard really isn’t that good of a fake beard at all, almost too obvious of a fake beard.
Based on a muddled script by SMJ (a playwright known only by their initials), this combination burlesque show and sexually-themed comedy is not only rude and crude but a fiasco.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this queer pirate romance, with some praising its swashbuckling fun and exploration of gender identity, while others find it confused, overly raunchy, and straying too far from the historical Anne Bonny and Mary Read story.
